utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Theunens, as well. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Jordash will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yesterday we were looking -- good morning, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yesterday we were, I think, dealing with your conclusions concerning the issue of tacit authorisation. Do you recall the issue?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And is this right -- we were looking at page 80 of the report, which is page 103 e-court. P1571 -- P1575. I beg your pardon. Are you there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and as I explained yesterday, this is a paragraph -- I mean, the paragraph we were discussing comes out of the summary of section 3, and I mean the basis for that summary can be found on the pages 83 to 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. No. I understand there's a -- you say there's support for that summary, but you're not saying the summary is incorrect, are you? The summary's a distillation of the evidence or a distillation of your analysis. So can we go to page 80, 103, and try to, if you could, explain which groups you say were tacitly authorised by the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explain in pages 83 to 89, there are a number of groups established by Serbian nationalistic political parties. In some documents they are identified as opposition parties, and they are supported -- or they are authorised to exist and tacitly supported by the government of Serbia, including the Ministry of Interior. And the support on the basis of the documents I review -- or this authorisation consists of the fact that the groups are allowed to be established. They are allowed to exist. There are documents indicating that they're allowed to organise themselves and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- I do understand that Mr. Jordash is asking identified those groups that were tacitly. What you are doing, you are explaining to us what the tacit acceptance or what was the tacit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- authorisation means. So Mr. Jordash is putting a different question, apparently, than you have in your mind. I could imagine that somewhere on page 85 we find a number of groups listed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, as Your Honours say there are a number of groups listed on the subparagraph B on page 85, and then I have referred to a number of documents where reference is made to some of these groups --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. Mr. Theunens can I stop you there.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So we can agree then, can we, that your tacit authorisation thesis - if I can put it like that - applies to the groups at least on page 85(b)?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, are there any other groups you identified which fall into the same category?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Thanks. We got there. So -- now, returning to page 80(D), 103 e-court, (D) also notes, and I'll read it again -- well, I'll read part of it again, the top of page 81. You're effectively saying that the Supreme Command, the JNA, the government of Serbia in particular the ministry of the MUP and the Ministry of Defence, not only were aware and effectively tacitly authorised, but also supported them otherwise. Now, which groups did you have in mind when you say the Serbian MUP support them otherwise?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, to give a very short answer to your question, I would like to draw your attention to page 94 where I discuss -- excuse me, page 94 of part 1 of the report where I discuss P1048, where reference is made -- I mean, it's a VJ security ODs report of October 1993, and there reference is made to, for example, paramilitary groups organised by the SPO, Serbian Renewal Movement, who according to this VJ security organs report have received weapons from the Serbian MUP. There's also reference made to in the same document paramilitary groups organised by the SRS, the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just stop you there a minute. What I'm interested in is not what individual -- at the moment what individual documents might say because obviously individual documents are part of a collection. What I'm interested in is your eventual conclusion after analysing all of these documents, what support was given to these groups which enabled you or made you conclude supported them otherwise? Which groups, what support?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents I have reviewed indicate the nature of the support for a number of groups, like for example P1048, I just identified. In addition if we take some distance from the individual documents, we come to the conclusion or we can draw the conclusion that, for example, groups controlled by the Serbian Radical Party were allowed to exist by the Ministry of Interior as a policy of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah. We've dealt with that Mr. Theunens, support to the group?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that if you allow a group to exist even though the law does not allow it, you provide support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, your report says supported them otherwise. So what we're talking about additional support?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. The support consists of you allowing them to exist, you allow them to organise themselves to recruit people. You provide weapons. You provide training. I mean, that happens at a later stage but there are indications, for example, that volunteers who initially were identified as volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were then trained in the -- yeah, the facility in Pajzos, in the vicinity of Bapska, Eastern Slavonia, before they were sent to municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in spring 1992 to participate in the takeover operations. And just could to conclude, as I try to explain the report, the support is part of the policy of the Serbian government and there we have, for example, the fact that these volunteers were treated on equal basis in relation to compensation for wounded and compensation also for -- I mean the time they didn't spend at their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's that got to do with the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serbian MUP is the Ministry of Interior's part of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So let me then take a step back. So you're -- are you conflating then the actions by the government with the actions of Serbian MUP throughout this report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. When you read my report, you will see that I -- whenever I can, I try to be as specific as possible, and I made a distinction between the support provided -- specific support by the MUP as well as the support provided by the government whereby for me the Serbian MUP, the Ministry of Interior is a part of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, but you're not suggesting that Serbian MUP was providing, or maybe you are, compensation for wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't suggested that in my report. As the report indicates and I think there is a document for that, it's part of a government policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's go back then. Okay. So that's a government policy. I want to go back to what support. You've said there's the tacit authorisation, and I want to deal specifically with Serbian MUP, not Serbian government, but Serbian MUP and the support you concluded it gave to these groups which were also tacitly authorised. You've told us about Seselj and training. What other support did you conclude had been given?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also mentioned arming, provisional weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To which groups?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is for example P1048 that identifies two groups whereby one is a very substantial group, namely the volunteers recruited and organised by the Serbian Radical Party, and this lasted for years not only in Croatia but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, when you have the law which prohibits the existence of such -- the establishment existence and so on of such groups and that law is not enforced, I understand that also as providing tacit support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But we've got that. We've got that. We're going to come to that later. I just want to clarify your conclusions. That -- so I understand them so I'm not heading off in the wrong direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep matters relatively simple. You asked what other support. The answer was provisional weapons and ammunition. Then the question was, to which groups, and then apparently the answers you took us to 1048, Serbian Radical Party over the years. Is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, and in addition also the groups organised by the Serbian Renewal Movement which are also mentioned in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The two groups mentioned in page 94 received in addition to the tacit authorisation apart from other matters arming as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So that's two. Any other group, any other support which fell within this conclusion at page 80 and 81?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- I wouldn't just see it as a matter of like numbers of groups. I would also look at the kind of groups. And as I tried to point out, groups organised by the Serbian Radical Party were the most prominent in the conflict in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina among the volunteers/paramilitary groups organised by nationalistic political parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's get ourselves organised in our thinking. The question was tacit authorisation and in addition to that other matters. Some were mentioned, like payment for wounded, and also arming. Then we focus on arming. We identified two specific groups that were assisted by being armed. Now, the next question: Any other group, any other support which fell within the conclusion? That immediately confuses us again, because we were talking about groups and the kind of support. We stopped at the kind of support specified as arming. We identified these two groups. Now, what other -- let's then -- either we start with the groups and say what other support did they get, or we start with the other type of support and ask ourselves what groups got that support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that there is some confusion, but Mr. Theunens is an experienced expert who is prone [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- and you're an experienced lawyer who puts questions in such a way. Any support -- any other group, any other support asks for confusion. Let's start with the other type of support, and it was provided to what group. Then we keep ourselves organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which other groups were provided with arms according to your conclusion, Mr. Theunens, by the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the documents -- I have reviewed, I'm not able to identify other groups organised by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that question was already put to the witness and was already answered by the witness. Do -- these are the two groups he identified as being armed on the basis of the documentation. Now, we move now to other support or other groups. Take it the way you want it, but not the two together, Mr. Jordash, because that other support, I think we have the payment of wounded soldiers by -- to what groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I tried to explain, this is a general policy which was introduced by the government of the Republic of Serbia and applied to all volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. All groups, you mentioned earlier the volunteer groups which are not the Dragan -- well, the three, the Dragan, the Arkan, and the -- okay. General policy to support for wounded soldiers and as it appeared from your earlier answer, not specifically MUP, general government policy. Okay, that's -- let's try to keep ourselves very organised in our minds. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Any other support provided by the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that earlier, but I want to repeat it. The fact that no legal action was undertaken against this group --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's the tacit authorisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would say if you allow a group to exist for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's support otherwise we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Let's -- tacit authorisation can take several forms. It being tacit means that you remain passive. You don't open your mouth. Now, then it's interesting to know under what circumstances, and I think, Mr. Theunens, you've mentioned that already, existence, recruitment, not responding, not taking any action if they were in operations or if they were seen to be active. Is that anything else in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the fact that these groups -- I mean, for example, the Serbian Radical Party establishes a war staff which recruits volunteers, and they do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We add to that open organisation of those groups in addition to existence. It's not only the groups existed, but they adopted the kind of an organisation and against this organisation also no action was taken. So we have now existence, organisation, recruitment, and the fourth was no response if they acted openly as a group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that you label as tacit authorisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- I mean, it started with tacit authorisation and then it develops into support, because if you allow a group to exist --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, okay. If that's -- I just want to clarify -- if that's right, okay, this -- the tacit authorisation and support, I want to just list the conclusions so I know what I'm dealing with, Mr. Theunens, please help me.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm desperately trying to help you, but I'm not sure whether you want to be helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's refrain from comment on who wants to be helped by whom. I do understand the answer of Mr. Theunens to be that the four elements he mentioned shows a process in which tacit authorisation goes beyond that and that in time the inactivity of the government to respond, that that takes the form of active support by doing nothing. That is how I understand your testimony, is that -- and you are nodding yes, for the record. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 80, 81, where we've been some time. What you've just described, the tacit authorisation is what led you to conclude, is it not, that these groups were encouraged.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tacit authorisation and the support encouraged the groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. And the support is included within the tacit authorisation and as we now know, the support is also, as you found, training and arming of Seselj's men, arming of the Serbian Renewal Movement. Anything else you had in mind when you made that conclusion on page 80, page 81?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refer to what Your Honours said just before your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which -- i.e., what?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Judge Orie said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So just --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He summarised my reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So we are limited then to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I left out the training, as a matter of fact, which you say took place later, but let's -- this is not -- words are important, Mr. Jordash, but it's not just the words. It's also trying to understand what is meant by those words, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, where the tacit authorisation moves into encouragement or -- I mean, that's to some extent is a matter of language, whereas that's of course a bit of a problem with an expert who tries to draw conclusions that the phrasing of the conclusions should be understood in the context of the basis on which these conclusions are drawn. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand your conclusion. So if there are no other types of support which you've concluded or meant to include within 80 and 81 then I can move on to the next section. Now, let's go to your CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we have P1574 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is this a fair summary, that the publications we see on page 3 -- sorry, page 2, beginning page 2 and on to page 3, all concern, apart from the first, issues relating to peacekeeping? Is that really where your academic interest lies?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have to go to the -- it's at the bottom of the second page, and it continues on the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, is that where your academic interest lies?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, you can qualify as academic interest, but -- I mean, most of the writing I did obviously when I was working at the Ministry of Defence in Belgium and doing peacekeeping missions. These are not academic publications but they are still relevant in the context of my current presence here, and that's -- you can find there a description at the last bullet point just before title 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is that -- your writing has been exclusively on peacekeeping issues other than publication 1, the role of military expertise and the Prosecution of and trials of international crimes?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My public writing as I tried to explain in my previous answer there you're correct, but obviously most of my writing was done, as I explained in my previous answer and was not public -- I'm sorry, published openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's go to page 3 of your -- I think that's where we are. Within the -- looking at your 1992 to 1998 and 1998 to 2000 entry there. "Within the Belgian military and during my participation in the aforementioned UN peacekeeping missions in the former Yugoslavia, I drafted numerous assessments and analysis on the situation in the former Yugoslavia, in particular in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina." What were these assessments?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are assessments on the situation in these countries, i.e., outlook for possible developments, predictive analysis on the possible developments for the political, military situation, as well as the security situation of Belgian peacekeepers who were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia at the time. And obviously when I was working the UN, this was not restricted to Belgian peacekeepers but to UNPROFOR and UNPF as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What does it mean to write a predictive analysis on the possible development? What does that process entail?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that you analyse the facts, i.e., the situation, the events that have occurred. You try to understand on the basis of those events and your overall understanding of the situation what can happen in the future in order to assist planning and decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who was supplying the facts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts -- I mean, I could give a very general answer. They are supplied by sources. I mean the information is provided by sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who generically are the sources?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A source is anybody or anything that can provide information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how did it work? How did the sources come to your office, if you like.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will -- for example, when working UNPROFOR, we received daily situation reports from the different levels because we were at the headquarters in Zagreb. So you have to -- had the operations headquarters for Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as FYROM, and then there's -- as you know, there's the whole structure with sectors, battalions and so -- and further on. We had access to open sources, i.e., summaries of local media. We would meet certain people. I, for example, I tried to go as much as possible to the field in order to discuss with not only blue helmets in the field but at occasions we could also meet members of the warring parties. I mean I, for example, had some meetings with the members of the during one visit 5th ABiH Corps. We may also have access to other information, and as I then explained yesterday, you applied the methodology in order to draft these protective analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the point of the predictive analysis was to assist with the peacekeeping mission?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was working in the UN, yes. In UNPROFOR, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how was it that you became employed by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- I'm not sure whether it was in December 2000 or January 2001. I saw a vacancy and I applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was the job specification?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know by heart any more, but I understood -- I mean, it was my impression that they looked for people -- the Office of the Prosecutor looked for intelligence analysts military, and I had the understanding that my background, my experience, professional/educational experience matched the requirements and I thought that it would be an interesting job, so I applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You hadn't had experience in combat yourself?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I was in the former Yugoslavia in UNPROFOR between -- I first went to former Yugoslavia, that's not in the CV, in August 1993. Bosnia-Herzegovina and also to Sector East in Croatia. Okay. We were not fired upon, but there were war operations ongoing in Bosnia-Herzegovina as you know very well. The same applies to UNPROFOR. During I -- for example, in December 1994 I went to Bihac with the logistics convoy and there was active fighting between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- is your question about being involved in combat operations yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what you are describing is being a witness or observing combat operations in which you were not involved yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try always to understand what the question is. For example, the last -- okay. That was your question, and that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've never fired a weapon in any combat?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your September -- looking at page 2 of your CV. September 1992 to June 1999, Balkans analyst. You were reporting -- sorry, you were following up and assessing the political and military and economic developments at the operational and strategic level. Was it just at the operational and strategic level that you were focusing on?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained in one of the articles I wrote, in a peacekeeping operation distinction between tactical, operational, and strategic can be very blurred. For example, a tactical development, i.e., a shooting incident near a check-point could immediately have operational or strategic implications. However, our assessments, the predictive analysis we prepared, focused on the operational and strategic level of command and control, i.e., the people I was working for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, when you started working for the ICTY Prosecution, what was your day-to-day job? Did it remain the same throughout your time or did it change?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, overall the job contents remained the same because I was -- during the eight years I was working here most of the times -- I mean, at least after 2002, most of the times in trial so I was conducting my analysis, for example, preparing expert reports. In addition, I was providing support to the trial team, OTP trial team, on the issues I highlighted in my CV, political background, military background. I participated in interviews of witnesses and suspects. In some trials I was called by the senior trial attorney to join him or her in the courtroom to assist with the examination and cross-examination of witnesses. So overall these were the kinds of activities I carried out during these eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you one of many military analysts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, I think there were like 10 or 12 in the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did that change?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team became -- the team became smaller over the -- over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And by -- by 2007, how big was the team?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no exact recollection. Maybe eight or nine. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there a hierarchy in the team?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in 2007 we still had a team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At the time of 2007, where were you in the team?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the military analysts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in 2007, was your day to day as you just described it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall -- I mean, the activities I mentioned, yes. At any given day these would be the activities depending on, for example, on trial schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So did you answer to a particular trial attorney or did you answer to all trial attorneys?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often I worked for several trial attorneys because I was working on several cases at the same time. Most of them were related cases, as you can see from my testimony in other trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which trial attorneys were you working for in 2007, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember some names. There was, I believe, Ms. Hildegard Retzlaff-Uertz was still here. I believe Mr. Marks Moore was here. I mean, it was the Vukovar trial. I'm not sure whether that was 2007 or 2008. I also worked for -- I mean, she wasn't a trial attorney -- a senior trial attorney, but Ms. Brehmeier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was working on this case at this time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly. There was -- I mean, there was also the Martic case, but I'm not sure whether the trial had finished. I would have to look at the dates when I testified, but anyway I was working for different senior trial attorneys at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And they could ask you, is this right, about -- for your assistance in relation to any aspect of their case preparation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, they wouldn't ask me for legal advice obviously, but if it concerned military issues or political even they would most often be better served by the experts in leadership research team, yeah they would contact me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But it could be for any aspect of the case preparation from advising on indictments to advising on court proceedings to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Clear questions, please. Advising on indictments is a rather ambiguous expression. What should be put in an indictment or how should an indictment should be phrased or how to -- you see, advising on an indictment is really something which confuses me. Could you please be more specific in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- with respect, I think advising on an indictment in the context of an expert opinion -- expert witness is quite specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it could -- it could mean what documentary evidence exists which could prove an indictment. It could also be what documentary evidence you are aware of which would support an indictment so as to advise on what to put in an indictment or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I understand that it could be many things, but unless I go through every single aspect of what advising could be, it would take me to ten minutes rather than, I'm hoping, putting something a little general Mr. Theunens can then answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens is now aware that part of your question, at least, is such that it could touch upon several aspects of what is phrased rather broadly. I interrupted you. Did you finish your question, Mr. Jordash or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll try to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you -- did you offer specialised knowledge to those engaged in drafting indictments?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on military aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there a pattern in terms of when you would be brought in to do that? At what stage of the drafting of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, because each -- what I remember, at least each senior trial attorney had his or her own approach, and in some cases I was not asked whatsoever or even if I spontaneously -- spontaneously proposed certain things irrespective of whether it was for an indictment or not, sometimes it was used, sometimes it was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, did the Prosecution -- did you see this indictment at the time it was being drafted, the Stanisic indictment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen it, but I have no clear recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You mean, throughout the whole of your time -- well, did you ever see the Stanisic indictment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of -- of course I saw it, because I read it before drafting my report in order to know which, for example, geographic areas I should cover, but I have no exact recollection whether I was involved in the -- in the drafting of the indictment, i.e., whether I was consulted or whether I gave, as you express, specialised knowledge on military issues during the drafting process. Probably I did, but as I explained earlier, I worked on sometimes five, six cases, among them sometimes two or three in the trial at the same time, and I didn't keep a detailed record of what I did for each trial at which -- or which case at which time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, did you not have notes concerning your interaction with the Stanisic indictment or with the Stanisic case in particular before you were asked to draft an expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My e-mails -- the e-mail exchanges would be the notes, but I did not keep separate notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you have e-mail exchanges. I mean, how much contact have you had with the Stanisic case before drafting the expert opinion in 2007?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to recollect exactly, because it's mainly related to persons. When Ms. Hildegard Retzlaff-Uertz was still here, obviously the case we were working on the Slobodan Milosevic case, Milan Martic, there were aspects that also touched upon this case, and there were several contacts as part of the two cases I mentioned. She left, and I'm not sure -- I think it was sometime in 2007. Then the contacts became much less. I was burdened with other cases. So then it was much more limited. So maybe once a week, once every fortnight. And as I said I was focused on that. I mean, we look at the dates, probably I was working mainly on Milan Martic case then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you were working on this case, though?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been part of the Prosecution team for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were -- you were interviewing witnesses or advising alongside the interviewing investigator or lawyer?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not -- I mean, at that time I don't recall that it was specifically for this case. I -- some of the witnesses I -- I think I participated in the interview of, say, two or three witnesses for -- in the Milan Martic case, some even during trial, and I didn't know -- I wouldn't know in advance whether they would be called here or not, or maybe they would appear as Defence witnesses. And the same applies to -- to other trials, other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Including this one.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what would that process entail, you sitting in on the interview?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could mean that I sat in on the interview, yes. It could also mean that I would draft questions which the lawyer or the investigator would use, yes or no. And it could also imply that I would ask questions. And I'm talking now in general. I have no specific recollection for -- for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what kind of questions would you draft in such situation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often my role consisted of identifying documents which would assist in understanding the background to the potential role of the witness or the activities of the witness. Sometimes they were documents signed by the witness we were about or the suspect we were about to interview. So I provided these -- I selected these documents. I tried to explain what they meant in the context. I mean, these were military documents. I think that's a good summary for what my role was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say "identify," you would do the searches on the various Prosecution databases and produce the documents and give them to the trial attorney or interviewing officer?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what would you looking for? Would you be looking for any document with the witness's name on it or inculpatory evidence or exculpatory evidence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't make any distinction, and I think especially the exculpatory evidence would be important because obviously we have a legal obligation to disclose that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you saw your duties as working -- when you were working for the OTP in that capacity to include the search for exculpatory material as a positive duty, did you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I see the role of -- of -- I mean, on my modest level of the OTP is try to identify the facts and not just one side of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that you cannot recall any of the detail of your interaction with the Stanisic case prior to your involvement writing an expert report? Is that really your evidence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. I have -- I have been involved in team meetings. I have participated in interviewing witnesses who may have been called here. I don't know. I don't know even -- I mean, I don't who has been called. I prepared memos on certain issues when I was asked, and okay, I did the work of a military analyst working for a trial team in the OTP. Or for a case team in the OTP. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So are we talking tens of hours or hundreds of hours of work on the Stanisic case prior to it, your drafting of the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take -- I mean, I started here in 2002, and obviously a lot of the work I did for, for example, the Slobodan Milosevic was of use here, too. Then I would more see it as hundreds of hours. But they were not specifically Stanisic and Simatovic. They were part of the overall package of tasks I carried out as a military analyst in the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, just trying to be a bit more specific. In relation to this case, in relation to the issues which pertain to this case -- well, let's stick with the first. In relation to this case specifically, can you estimate, is it tens or hundreds of hours? This case specifically.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it would be more tens, tens of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to the issues which pertain to this case such as the Red Berets, such as Martic, such as the various paramilitaries you've identified, we are talking hundreds of hours?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And even -- I mean, you go tens, hundreds. It's a wide range.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I've been quoted as saying which is the Red Berets such as Martic, and I think what I meant to say the Red Berets as well as Martic. Sorry, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I didn't keep count of the hours, but I can say that I worked on this case before, most of the time because it was related to other cases I was working on for a long time. Preparing a report takes -- I means, it's not a question of tens of hours. It's hundreds of hours to prepare such a report. But I what I'm trying to explain is that it was specific time I dedicated to this case, no. It was part of the overall package where, as you will compare -- when you compare this report with like the Seselj report I did for the Seselj case or Martic or Milosevic, there is some similarity obviously. I didn't have to reinvent everything. A lot of material was already reviewed. I had already reviewed a lot of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in relation to all of these hundreds of hours, you saw it as your duty to continuously identify exculpatory material?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's part of my daily job, and if I would discover such material I would send it to the trial team because they would deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, let's move to when you were first approached in this case to write a report. Who did you first meet?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, in the very early stages Ms. Hildegard Retzlaff-Uertz spoke about the requirement for -- in this case there would have to be a report too. That was -- that is several years before 2007, but I didn't work it on, but then in 2007 Ms. Brehmeier told me that the trial team requested an expert -- a military expert report for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And they asked you to write a report to -- within which parameters?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initial parameters were extremely general. It was basically write a military expert report and then I proposed, okay I will submit a table of contents for your review, and that table of contents will then serve as my -- my direction or the guidance for my further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, go on. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. So I submitted a draft table of contents and that was approved and that's when I started to -- I mean, continued to work on the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to Exhibit P1575 MFI'd and to page 2 of the table of contents, and it's 16 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, are you able at this stage to identify which were the headings that you first sat down and drafted before beginning the drafting of the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I adopted -- or I -- it was my intention to take the same structure I had or the same approach I had applied in the other cases, i.e., to have -- to see whether at least have two big components in the report, first a background section which would deal with legislation, doctrine, and related issues, and then call it a factual section which would deal with the situation as it unfolded during -- during the conflict in Croatia and the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that explains part 1. And then okay because the volume -- it was too voluminous I split Croatia Bosnia-Herzegovina in two separate parts, part 2 and part 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what about the sub-heading. Let's take for example at page 3, 17 on e-court, "Serbian Volunteer/Paramilitary Groups."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was that one of the subheadings which you took from other reports?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have done or -- I mean, discussed such issues also in my report for the Seselj case. I'm not sure whether -- to what extent I used the same title in the Milosevic case, because over the years we acquired more material, and so I was able to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the title below that, "Serbian Volunteers/Paramilitary Groups Controlled by or Linked Otherwise to the Ministry of Interior Republic of Serbia," how did that heading materialise and at what point?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When conducting the research and drafting the report, and I did it in a way like I could draft maybe one section of part 3 and then go back to a section part 2 depending on the time I had available and other issues, I came to a conclusion that there were groups which had specific relations with the Ministry of Interior, but I was not able on the basis of the material I had available to provide a general definition like, okay, command and control, and so I took a bit of a maybe more general definition or title in which I tried to encompass the different aspects of that relation as I identified it on the basis of the documents I reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you're saying that heading wasn't there when you first showed Ms. Brehmeier the contents table.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's no reference to Ms. Brehmeier here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, didn't you say yesterday that you'd shown an OTP representative the draft headings?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Ms. Brehmeier as I confirmed today, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm not sure whether all the headings as they are in the final table of contents were all there. I'm pretty sure they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Because you said yesterday Ms. Brehmeier hadn't made any substantive alterations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you let me finish. I don't remember any feed -- specific feedback except for, yeah, it's okay, to the table of contents. But as I tried to explain, once I had the table of -- or the overall table of contents, then my work only starts, and obviously I can still make changes, it's my report. So -- and I had to explain that also in another trial here, that the headings reflect the contents. So it could well be that I would change a heading after I had finished a section because only then after reviewing the material that was available to me I could draw a conclusion as to what that material meant to me, and this may be one of these conclusions. I mean, one of the headings that was established in such a manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You don't -- you don't know at this stage. You don't know whether it was there in the initial draft you gave to Ms. Brehmeier or it was something that came later?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I'm very sure Ms. Brehmeier had no influence whatsoever on the nature on the contents of the table of contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting she did. I'm asking -- you're not able to say whether that title was there at the beginning or it came later.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to see the draft I submitted to her. I didn't have the time to review all the draft before I came here, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You have the draft, do you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be in the OTP. I mean, when I left I didn't erase my hard disk or something or the network so the material is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But let me -- let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honour. I don't know if?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would have a bit of a different time schedule this morning, not having sessions of 75 minutes but two sessions each, approximately 60 minutes. If this would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just ask one or two last questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll adduct the time we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You don't have a recollection, though, of going back to her, Ms. Brehmeier, or any other OTP representative with new titles, including this title, "The Serbian Volunteer/Paramilitary Groups Controlled by or Related Otherwise to the MUP of Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is as follows: I submitted a -- when I got the tasking, within a week or two I submitted a draft table of contents which was very similar to this one but obviously there were a lot of gaps. And then more or less a week or a number of days before the deadline that was established by the Trial Chamber, I submitted a draft report to Ms. Brehmeier, and I received that draft report back with the only comments like there were some typos in it, and those are the only contacts I had with the Stanisic-Simatovic OTP trial team on this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't remember, you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you don't remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you gave us the information which you still remember and what you don't remember, and that's what Mr. Jordash is talking about. If you don't remember further details about that, then you don't remember, and that seems to be a -- an unproblematic matter. We will have a break, and we will resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to move swiftly and wrap up this section, Mr. Theunens. Just some clarification. Was there e-mail exchange between you and Ms. Brehmeier during the drafting of your report concerning the drafting of your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent the draft table of contents by e-mail. I'm not -- I don't remember whether I got her feedback that she agreed with the nature -- or the table -- the draft table of contents, whether I got that orally or by e-mail, and I submitted the draft report to her, I mean the final draft, to her by e-mail, and again I don't remember -- I mean, she -- no, she replied to me, I mean, with the draft saying there was some typos line whatever in this part, this word or that word, and that was also done by e-mail. I don't recall any other e-mails concerning the drafting of the report in between these two e-mails.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Nor with any other Prosecutor involved in the Stanisic case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And just to be fully accurate, there may have been e-mail exchanges on the progress of the work like I remember there were hearings in the -- in the case where the Trial Chamber invited Ms. Brehmeier to propose deadlines when the expert reports would be submitted, and I may have received an e-mail from her asking me when would report be finished or whether I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to cut this short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash is apparently seeking whether there was any exchange of substantial comments on drafts you produced, and I take it from your answer that it was rather practical matters than anything else, and is that the full answer to the question? If that's the case, then you can move on, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just so that we understand the process which you followed, was the first step to sit in front of the various databases and search on the subjects which had been identified in your table of contents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first step was see what I had already done, i.e., reports for other trials, cutting and pasting that in a draft report, and then identifying key words or -- yeah, key words I would use to conduct searches. Identifying what I would call information gaps and based on that also, yeah, the key words to conduct the searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the key words to fill the information gaps produced a number of documents, and then how did you make the selection of which documents would go into the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I made the selection by applying the methodology I explained yesterday. For each and every document I saw, I would obviously evaluate the documents, i.e., I would look at the reliability of the source, the credibility of the information. I would try to find when I had a document saying one thing, I would try to find another document that would corroborate that information or not in order to make sure -- I mean, again to ascertain the credibility of the information. And it's basically like a puzzle where you identify pieces, and by conducting additional searches additional pieces can be identified and a picture is being created at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And so did that process then involve a rejection of documents which you didn't find reliable?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rejection in a sense of not including them in the report, but I would still keep them with me, because obviously over the years the OTP acquired additional documentary evidence, and it could be that information that seemed less credible at one moment because of the availability of additional documents, that that information would become more credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, was there, though, at the end of your -- the process whereby you completed your draft, a pile of documents which had not found its -- their way into the report because you hadn't found them reliable or convincing or useful, and then a pile of documents which you had found to be so, and you put those in the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's -- that's the way how you could represent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that process from what you've told us then necessarily would have involved finding exculpatory material; correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, when I conduct the searches on the basis of the key words I discover different materials, and material that looked exculpatory, i.e., Rule 68, would I share that with the team. I would forward it to the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you put it -- or did that exculpatory material find its way into the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you indicate where that is? Just a paragraph or two where you deal with documents and a conclusion or a comment on those documents which is exculpatory in terms of the accused's liability or the Serbian MUP's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a specific paragraph or conclusion to that effect. But there are, for example, situations when I had only -- no, when there was a contradictory conclusion as to the nature of a unit, was it the MUP RS, MUP RSK, or MUP Serbia unit, I would highlight what the different document said. I mean, it's not a hundred per cent exculpatory, but at least I tried to be as accurate as possible to -- as in case there is any doubt about, for example, here the allegiance or the adherence of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you didn't include any paragraph, or you didn't come to any conclusions, let me put it that way, you didn't come to any conclusions yourself on the basis of a perusal and assessment of the documents which undermine the inference that the MUP was responsible for that the accused were responsible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a question of the logic you apply. I mean, the conclusion is the result of the materials you look at, and -- I mean, the materials can say different things. I will try to draw a conclusion on the basis of the materials I have in front of me, but it's not that you have a preconceived conclusion, and then you would try to do the opposite. That doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the simple answer is that you didn't draw any conclusions which you placed into the report which undermine the responsibility of the MUP or the accused's responsibility. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a bit of a too drastic conclusion. For example, I have included documents indicating that indeed the MUP acted against paramilitaries at a certain moment in time. You could consider that material exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But did you draw that conclusion, though, and say well, for this period of time I can say the Serbian MUP did fulfil its duties, for example. Did you draw that conclusion and put it in the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I'm just trying to identify it. When we talk about Article 118 of the Law of Defence of the Republic of Serbia on the prohibition of the organisation, establishment, and so on of paramilitary groups, I state that this article was selectively implemented by the Ministry of Interior. Now, you could say this is exculpatory because it shows that they do implement it, but they do it selectively, but I found it important to include that document to show that they had the ability to implement the article, and I -- it's on page 93 of part 1 where I refer to -- it's P1057.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So what conclusion did you reach then concerning the exculpatory part of that conclusion? What did the Ministry of the Interior do as you found it in relation to its obligations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: P1057 shows that the Ministry of the Interior -- I mean the police arrested a leader of a paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was that then the full extent of your conclusion concerning the exculpatory aspect of this selective enforcement conclusion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I can see that the arrest of a leader of a paramilitary group could be viewed as exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can see how the selective enforcement has an exculpatory aspect to it, but did you reach any other conclusions concerning what the Serbian MUP did other than the arrest of one leader?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, on the same page there is P1058 where I indicate that the state security collected the information on the activities of at least one volunteer group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. So that's two things. Anything else that you concluded having looked at all these databases that you had in your possession, all the hundreds of documents you must have looked at.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I looked at many documents in accordance with the methodology I explained yesterday, and more specifically the table of contents I had. So when I tried to explain, for example, I have a section on relations or -- I mean, we still have the table of contents titled "4. Serbian Volunteer/Paramilitary Groups," and I look at attitude of the authority of the SFRY, of course I take all these aspects into account to the best of my abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not explicitly looking for inculpatory or exculpatory conclusions. I'm trying to draw conclusions on the basis -- I have the facts -- on the basis of the facts that are established in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the only then - is this right? - document you saw, and perhaps I should say thousands of documents that you've looked at over the years and prior to 2007, out of the thousands of documents you saw the only two documents which suggested that the Serbian MUP did anything in relation to paramilitary groups in enforcing the prohibition on them as you see it is those two documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report is a selection of material. So I didn't include -- I mean, if I want to use your terminology, I didn't include all the inculpatory material. I tried to identify the most significant documents again to understand the facts in order for me to draw certain conclusions. And I didn't look specifically at the nature of these documents, except if it was an exculpatory document, my first concern or my -- I mean the important concern was to send it to the team because it had to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to that in more concrete form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question, Mr. Theunens. I'll read part of your answer to one of the previous questions as it appears on my screen. You said you tried to identify -- you said that Article 118 of the law of the defence of the Republic of Serbia was selectively implemented by the Ministry of Interior. Yes. And then you continued and I now literally quote: "Now, you say -- could say this is exculpatory because it shows that they do implement it, but they do it selectively, but I found it important to include that document to show that they had the ability to implement the article." And then you give the source. Your answer puzzled me because you say drawing the attention to the selective implementation you could consider that as exculpatory because they did implement it, although not always. And then you continue by saying: "But I found it important to include that document to show that they had the ability to implement the article," which is inculpatory to the extent that not implementing due to a lack of ability may be neutral or -- but not implementing where you have shown the ability might well be understood as very inculpatory. And I was puzzled by your answer saying now you could say it's exculpatory, but I found it important to show the ability which tends to be more inculpatory or at least the inculpatory elements seems to be more on the foreground and you make the distinction between exculpatory and this aspect which, although you do not say that with that many words, could easily be understood as inculpatory. Could you -- because I was puzzled by the answer because I wondered to what extent it shows a mindset.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should have included -- I'm not sure what said but I should have said, "but I also found it important to include the document." Now, as I tried to explain to Mr. Jordash, the starting point is not to say I look for inculpatory or exculpatory material. The starting point is to -- is to identify material that allows to understand the role in this case of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia in relation to volunteer/paramilitaries, and I came across various documents, and the most the documents I consider the most significant I included in the report, significant in the sense that allows to understand what the Ministry of the Interior was doing in relation these volunteers and paramilitaries. The issue we're discussing now, i.e., whether it's inculpatory or exculpatory, as I said was not my primary concern. I tried to provide a complete picture in order to understand the role. Now, these conclusions -- I mean you can look at each document individually, and you could say, okay, this is more inculpatory, this is more exculpatory, but that's not the process I conducted. That was not my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the difference if you would have given the answer, but I also found it important that's not what is recorded as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's, but it certainly would have -- my question would have been phrased quite differently if the word "also" had appeared there. I was puzzled by the answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. So I just want to understand the situation. We have on page 93 the two exhibits you've just referred to, I think, showing this selective enforcement, so showing some enforcement by the Serbian MUP. Now, is it the fact that you didn't find any other enforcement by the MUP or you found other enforcement and you didn't find those documents reliable, or you simply didn't -- you found documents of Serbian MUP enforcement but just chose not to include them for another reason.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that there was additional -- or there was enforcement, for example, in November 1993. I mean, there are documents about that from the Serbian Radical Party, and I believe also from the MUP whereby senior volunteers of the republican -- of the Serbian Radical Republican Party are arrested. I don't think I included those in my report here. I include them in another report. Okay, it's not relevant for this trial, but again they would also have shown the selective implementation of Article 118, and again for reasons -- reasons of concisivness I chose not to include those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You accept they would have been exculpatory. I mean, it's a matter of degree how much, but do you accept that they would have been exculpatory?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it would have been a separate a separate analysis because again if we go into the specifics of these documents we see that people were indeed arrested but they were almost immediately released, and they were only arrested as we see with P1057 on the basis of illegal possession of firearms, whereas there was information available from various sources that these volunteers had been involved in serious crimes. And again I chose for reasons of concisivness not to include these documents or to refer to that specific aspect in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So apart from then Seselj -- they arrested the Seselj members in 1993 for what you would see as the wrong reasons or the wrong charges, and these two documents in here, you didn't find anything else which showed what the Serbian MUP might have been doing relevant to this report or to this issue in the report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean obviously I conducted searches, for example, when I had a JNA report, I mean, a security [indiscernible] report on alleged crimes by Arkan, I did conduct searches to try to see whether the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia carried out any action in relation to those or other reports on -- on illegal activities conducted by Arkan, and I don't remember finding any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please if you have them show me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will in due course, Mr. Theunens. Did you ask -- I mean, we'll come back to this in more detail when I take you through the legislation, but just to wrap this point up now, you did say yesterday, I think, in relation to my learned friend Mr. Weber, your approach had not been to analyse - am I stating this fairly? - analyse the Ministry of the Interior and its workings? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Weber asked me about the structure of the Ministry of the Interior and indeed I didn't analyse that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you analyse -- well, let me put it differently. Did you ask anyone in the OTP to write to the National Council and ask for documents showing what the Ministry of the Interior was doing in these years?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have even myself, I mean, drafted a draft RFAs, request for assistance, on the issues you highlighted and for me that was essential not just for this particular but also for other trials I was working on; i.e., reports on investigation of volunteers/paramilitaries and any trial cases that was happening, because to me that is an essential aspect of -- would be an essential aspect of what were my tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you wrote an RFA asking the National Council to produce the work diaries or the daily reports, the weekly reports, the annual reports, from the Ministry of Interior of Serbia to show what they were doing between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I drafted several RFAs in relation to these documents prepared by the military. As you know, there were several -- I mean, I haven't -- I don't remember drafting any specific RFAs for the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you have your records with you in The Hague, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have them with me. I mean, I left here and -- but it's all on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's all on the record.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the Prosecution should have the RFAs, if they exist, where you wrote to the MUP and the response which produced whatever it produced.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself, I didn't keep a record of the response. I kept a record of the documents I drafted, but -- I mean, I'm certain I drafted several RFAs in relation, for example, to Vukovar case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But, Mr. Theunens, sorry to interrupt, but this was -- did you not see this as an essential part of your analysis in this -- the compilation for this report? I am setting out to draft a report what it was the MUP should have done, what it was they didn't do, and what the consequences of that failure led to. So do you not have a very clear recollection of your investigative approach in terms of seeking out the information to show what the Serbian MUP did?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure I drafted such RFAs for what the military is concerned, I mean, the JNA, the SFRY Armed Forces, and the VJ. I am not sure -- I mean, you would have to check -- you would have to check my work records whether I drafted some -- such RFAs for the Serbian Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave the point now. We'll come back to it later when we look at documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have please on e-court P321 -- sorry, P327.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just understand the process a security officer had a duty at that time in classical JNA military doctrine had a duty to investigate crime within the JNA by JNA military personnel, or by armed forces personnel?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would first like to finish my answer to the previous question where I was saying that we know -- I mean it has been established that the security administration at the SSNO, i.e., the addressee of the report, was very interested in the activities of various paramilitaries, i.e., nonofficial armed forces knowing that the armed forces consist of the JNA and the TO. Coming to your second question, yeah, security officers had among their duties, I mean their duties included among other duties to investigate crimes; for example, crimes against the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And by armed forces personnel?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the way it would work is that the crime would be -- there would be some evidence of the crime and the security organ in that particular military unit or military region would then set off and investigate that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an example of -- of what a security organ could do among its other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: They might instruct, for example, the military police to take action, too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what might the military police -- what might the military police do? In a situation like this, what would this -- let me start this again. In a situation like this, what would -- what would the duty of the security officer be?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: About which situation are we talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Arkan.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, and what about Mr. Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, he's investigating Arkan or she is investigating Arkan. What would his duty be?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean it depends how -- this is not an example of a criminal investigation report. As you know, I have included some of these reports for the situation Saborsko and Skabrnja where security organs use a particular template to -- when they are -- when they're providing an investigative report, this document does not correspond with the template. It's an information report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the difference is that there is no investigation of a specific event, and if you -- I mean, I will try -- I will identify the pages where I highlight -- where I show these investigative reports, again with a specific template. Here the security organ is providing information on what Arkan is doing, and on the basis of that information, if there's clear reference to a crime, they would have prepared an investigative report, but it has a different -- it looks different. It's a different kind of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the information report at page 1 which we have on the screen identifies a crime by Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- I'm -- again that may be my mistake. I'm a bit confused. My understanding of the words "security" and "investigations" leads me to make the following observation: I am under the impression, and I am seeking verification of that because that's what we're here for and not to work on the basis of my personal impressions, that activity by security organs and security staff is primarily aiming at gathering information which is important for tactical operation -- whatever; whereas, investigations conducted by police, military police included, is primarily aiming at establishing facts for the purpose of deciding whether or not to further proceed against a person who may have committed a crime.
